Chapter 2 - Quadratics.correct_answer: $$(a)\ a=1,b=3,c=1\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{-3\pm\sqrt{9-4}}{2}=\dfrac{-3\pm\sqrt5}{2}.$$ $$(b)\ a=1,b=-3,c=-2\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{3\pm\sqrt{9+8}}{2}=\dfrac{3\pm\sqrt{17}}{2}.$$ $$(c)\ a=1,b=6,c=6\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{-6\pm\sqrt{36-24}}{2}=\dfrac{-6\pm\sqrt{12}}{2}=-3\pm\sqrt3.$$ $$(d)\ a=1,b=-5,c=-2\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{5\pm\sqrt{25+8}}{2}=\dfrac{5\pm\sqrt{33}}{2}.$$ $$(e)\ a=3,b=10,c=-2\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{-10\pm\sqrt{100+24}}{6}=\dfrac{-10\pm\sqrt{124}}{6}=\dfrac{-10\pm2\sqrt{31}}{6}=\dfrac{-5\pm\sqrt{31}}{3}.$$ $$(f)\ a=4,b=-4,c=-1\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{16+16}}{8}=\dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{32}}{8}=\dfrac{4\pm4\sqrt2}{8}=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt2}{2}.$$ $$(g)\ 4x^{2}-7x-2=0,\ a=4,b=-7,c=-2\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{7\pm\sqrt{49+32}}{8}=\dfrac{7\pm\sqrt{81}}{8}=\dfrac{7\pm9}{8}\Rightarrow x=2,\ -\tfrac14.$$ $$(h)\ a=11,b=2,c=-7\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{-2\pm\sqrt{4+308}}{22}=\dfrac{-2\pm\sqrt{312}}{22}=\dfrac{-2\pm2\sqrt{78}}{22}=\dfrac{-1\pm\sqrt{78}}{11}.$$

Give your answers to three significant figures: (a) $$x^{2}+4x+2=0$$ (b) $$x^{2}-8x+1=0$$ (c) $$x^{2}+11x-9=0$$ (d) $$x^{2}-7x-17=0$$ (e) $$5x^{2}+9x-1=0$$ (f) $$2x^{2}-3x-18=0$$ (g) $$3x^{2}+8=16x$$ (h) $$2x^{2}+11x=5x^{2}-18$$.
Chapter 2 - Quadratics.hint: Apply $$x=\dfrac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{2a}$$ to each, then evaluate the roots numerically and round to 3 s.f.
Chapter 2 - Quadratics.correct_answer: $$(a)\ a=1,b=4,c=2\Rightarrow x=-2\pm\sqrt2\Rightarrow x\approx-0.586,-3.41.$$ $$(b)\ a=1,b=-8,c=1\Rightarrow x=4\pm\sqrt{15}\Rightarrow x\approx7.87,0.127.$$ $$(c)\ a=1,b=11,c=-9\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{-11\pm\sqrt{157}}{2}\Rightarrow x\approx0.765,-11.8.$$ $$(d)\ a=1,b=-7,c=-17\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{7\pm\sqrt{117}}{2}\Rightarrow x\approx8.91,-1.91.$$ $$(e)\ a=5,b=9,c=-1\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{-9\pm\sqrt{101}}{10}\Rightarrow x\approx0.105,-1.90.$$ $$(f)\ a=2,b=-3,c=-18\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{3\pm\sqrt{153}}{4}\Rightarrow x\approx3.84,-2.34.$$ $$(g)\ 3x^{2}-16x+8=0,\ a=3,b=-16,c=8\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{16\pm\sqrt{160}}{6}\Rightarrow x\approx4.77,0.559.$$ $$(h)\ 3x^{2}-11x-18=0,\ a=3,b=-11,c=-18\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{11\pm\sqrt{337}}{6}\Rightarrow x\approx4.89,-1.23.$$

Chapter 2 - Quadratics.question_text: Show that solving $$x^2 + 2bx + c = 0$$ by completing the square gives $$x = -b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - c}.$$
Chapter 2 - Quadratics.correct_answer: $$x^2 + 2bx = -c \Rightarrow (x + b)^2 - b^2 = -c \Rightarrow (x + b)^2 = b^2 - c \Rightarrow x + b = \pm \sqrt{b^2 - c} \Rightarrow x = -b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - c}.$$

Chapter 2 - Quadratics.question_text: Sketch $$y=x^2-6x+8$$: show intercepts, turning point, and line of symmetry.
Chapter 2 - Quadratics.correct_answer: Intercepts: $$y\text{-int }(0,8),\ x\text{-ints from }(x-2)(x-4)=0\Rightarrow(2,0),(4,0).$$ Vertex: $$x_v=\frac{6}{2}=3,\ y_v=3^2-6\cdot3+8=-1\Rightarrow(3,-1).$$ Line of symmetry: $$x=3.$$

Chapter 2 - Quadratics.question_text: Sketch $$y=x^2+2x-15$$: show intercepts, turning point, and line of symmetry.
Sketch $$y=25-x^2$$: show intercepts, turning point, and line of symmetry.
Chapter 2 - Quadratics.correct_answer: Intercepts: $$y\text{-int }(0,25),\ x\text{-ints from }25-x^2=0\Rightarrow x=\pm5\Rightarrow(-5,0),(5,0).$$ Vertex: $$x_v=0,\ y_v=25\Rightarrow(0,25).$$ Axis: $$x=0.$$

Chapter 2 - Quadratics.question_text: Sketch $$y=x^2+3x+2$$: show intercepts, turning point, and line of symmetry.
Sketch $$y=-x^2+6x+7$$: show intercepts, turning point, and line of symmetry.
Chapter 2 - Quadratics.correct_answer: Intercepts: $$y\text{-int }(0,7),\ x\text{-ints from }-x^2+6x+7=0\Rightarrow x^2-6x-7=0\Rightarrow x=-1,7\Rightarrow(-1,0),(7,0).$$ Vertex: $$x_v=-\frac{6}{2(-1)}=3,\ y_v=-(3)^2+6(3)+7=16\Rightarrow(3,16).$$ Axis: $$x=3.$$

Chapter 2 - Quadratics.question_text: Sketch $$y=2x^2+4x+10$$: show intercepts, turning point, and line of symmetry.
Sketch $$y=2x^2+7x-15$$: show intercepts, turning point, and line of symmetry.
Sketch $$y=6x^2-19x+10$$: show intercepts, turning point, and line of symmetry.
Chapter 2 - Quadratics.hint: Quadratic formula for roots; vertex via $$-b/(2a)$$.
Chapter 2 - Quadratics.correct_answer: Intercepts: $$y\text{-int }(0,10),\ x\text{-ints from }6x^2-19x+10=0\Rightarrow x=\tfrac{2}{3},\ \tfrac{5}{2}\Rightarrow\left(\tfrac{2}{3},0\right),\left(\tfrac{5}{2},0\right).$$ Vertex: $$x_v=\frac{19}{12},\ y_v=6\left(\tfrac{19}{12}\right)^2-19\left(\tfrac{19}{12}\right)+10=-\tfrac{121}{24}\Rightarrow\left(\tfrac{19}{12},-\tfrac{121}{24}\right).$$ Axis: $$x=\tfrac{19}{12}.$$

Chapter 2 - Quadratics.question_text: Sketch $$y=4-7x-2x^2$$: show intercepts, turning point, and line of symmetry.
Chapter 2 - Quadratics.correct_answer: Intercepts: $$y\text{-int }(0,4),\ x\text{-ints from }-2x^2-7x+4=0\Rightarrow2x^2+7x-4=0\Rightarrow x=-4,\ \tfrac{1}{2}\Rightarrow(-4,0),\left(\tfrac{1}{2},0\right).$$ Vertex: $$x_v=-\frac{-7}{2(-2)}=-\tfrac{7}{4},\ y_v=-2\left(-\tfrac{7}{4}\right)^2-7\left(-\tfrac{7}{4}\right)+4=\tfrac{81}{8}\Rightarrow\left(-\tfrac{7}{4},\tfrac{81}{8}\right).$$ Axis: $$x=-\tfrac{7}{4}.$$

Chapter 2 - Quadratics.hint: Use discriminant: two distinct roots iff $$\Delta=b^2-4ac>0$$.

Given $$f(x)=5x^2+8x+s$$ has equal roots, find the positive constant $$s$$.
Find the range of $$k$$ for which $$3x^2-4x+k=0$$ has no real solutions.

Chapter 2 - Quadratics.hint: Set discriminant to zero and solve for integer $$p$$.

Chapter 2 - Quadratics.question_text: For $$h(x)=2x^2+(k+4)x+k,$$ find the discriminant in terms of $$k$$.
Hence, or otherwise, prove that $$h(x)=2x^2+(k+4)x+k$$ has two distinct real roots for all real $$k$$.
Chapter 2 - Quadratics.hint: Use the discriminant found: two distinct roots iff $$\Delta>0$$.
Chapter 2 - Quadratics.correct_answer: Since $$\Delta=k^2+16\ge16>0$$ for all $$k\in\mathbb R,$$ the equation always has **two distinct real roots**.

Chapter 2 - Quadratics.question_text: (a) A car model is $$y=-0.01x^2+0.975x+16\ (x>0)$$ mpg. Find the two speeds at which $$y=32.5$$ mpg.
( b) Rewrite $$y=-0.01x^2+0.975x+16$$ in the form $$A-B(x-C)^2$$ and state $$A,B,C$$.
(c) Using the form in part (b), find the speed with greatest fuel efficiency.
Chapter 2 - Quadratics.hint: Maximum at the vertex of a downward parabola.
Chapter 2 - Quadratics.correct_answer: Since $$y=A-B(x-C)^2$$ with $$B>0,$$ the maximum occurs at $$x=C=48.75\text{ mph}$$ (max mpg $$=A=39.765625$$).

Chapter 2 - Quadratics.question_text: Use the model to find fuel consumption at $$x=120$$ mph and comment on validity at very high speeds.
Chapter 2 - Quadratics.correct_answer: $$y=-0.01(120)^2+0.975(120)+16=-144+117+16=-11\text{ mpg}.$$ A negative mpg is not physically meaningful ⇒ the quadratic model is unreliable at very high speeds; it is valid only over a moderate speed range.

Chapter 2 - Quadratics.question_text: (a) A fertiliser model $$g=6+0.03f-0.00006f^2$$ (tonnes/ha) gives yield for fertiliser $$f$$ (kg/ha). According to the model, how much grain per hectare with no fertiliser?
(b) One farmer currently uses $$f=20$$ kg/ha. How much **additional** fertiliser is needed to increase yield by 1 tonne/ha?
Chapter 2 - Quadratics.hint: Target $$g=6.576+1=7.576$$; solve for $$f$$ and choose the realistic root.
Chapter 2 - Quadratics.correct_answer: Current $$g(20)=6+0.03(20)-0.00006(20)^2=6.576.$$ Solve $$6+0.03f-0.00006f^2=7.576\Rightarrow -0.00006f^2+0.03f-1.576=0$$ ⇒ $$f\approx59.65\text{ or }440.35.$$ The realistic choice near 20 is $$f\approx59.65,$$ so **additional** fertiliser $$\approx59.65-20=39.65\text{ kg/ha}$$ (≈$$39.6$$ kg/ha).

Chapter 2 - Quadratics.question_text: A football stadium has 25,000 seats. The football club knows from experience that they will sell 10,000 tickets if each ticket costs £30. They also expect to sell 1,000 more tickets for every £1 the price decreases. (a) The number of tickets sold, $$t$$, can be modelled by the linear equation $$t=M-1000p$$, where £$$p$$ is the price of each ticket and $$M$$ is a constant. Find the value of $$M$$.

(b) The total revenue (£$$r$$) can be calculated by multiplying the number of tickets sold by the price of each ticket. This gives $$r=p(M-1000p)$$. Rewrite this in the form $$A-B(p-C)^2,$$ where $$A,B,C$$ are constants to be found.
(c) Using the revenue equation or otherwise, determine how much the football club should charge per ticket to make the maximum amount of money.
Chapter 2 - Quadratics.hint: Maximum occurs at the vertex when $$p=C$$.
Chapter 2 - Quadratics.correct_answer: From $$r=400000-1000(p-20)^2,$$ the maximum occurs at $$p=20.$$ Therefore, the club should charge **£20 per ticket** for maximum revenue.

Chapter 2 - Quadratics.question_text: Lynn sold 80 cushions at £15 each. She expects to sell 10 more cushions for every £1 the price decreases. (a) The number sold is modelled by $$c=230-Hp$$ where £$$p$$ is the price and $$H$$ is a constant. Determine $$H$$.
Chapter 2 - Quadratics.hint: Substitute the known point into the model.

Chapter 2 - Quadratics.question_text: Lynn’s revenue is $$r=p(230-Hp)$$. Using $$H=10$$, (b) rewrite in the form $$A-B(p-C)^2$$ and state $$A,B,C$$.
(c) Using the form in part (b) or otherwise, show Lynn can increase revenue by £122.50 by lowering the price, and state the optimum selling price.
Chapter 2 - Quadratics.hint: Compare current revenue with the vertex value.
Chapter 2 - Quadratics.correct_answer: Current revenue at £15: $$r_0=15\times80=1200.$$ From $$r=1322.5-10(p-11.5)^2,$$ maximum revenue is $$A=1322.5$$ at $$p=C=11.5.$$ Increase: $$1322.5-1200=£122.5.$$ Therefore, lowering the price to **£11.50** maximises revenue and increases it by **£122.50**.

Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.correct_answer: From second $$x=5+2ky$$; sub into first $$3(5+2ky)+ky=8\Rightarrow15+7ky=8\Rightarrow y=-\tfrac{1}{k},\ x=3.$$

Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.question_text: (b) Given also $$y=\tfrac12$$, find $$k$$.
The system $$\begin{cases}2x-py=5\\4x+5y+q=0\end{cases}$$ has $$x=q,\ y=-1.$$ Find $$p,q$$.
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.correct_answer: From first $$2q+p=5$$, from second $$5q-5=0\Rightarrow q=1,\ p=3.$$

Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.question_title: Draw graphs of two linear equations
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.question_text: $$\text{Use graph paper to draw accurately the graphs of }2y=2x+11\text{ and }y=2x^2-3x-5\text{ on the same axes}$$
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.hint: $$\text{Rewrite each equation in the form }y=\dots\text{ and plot key points clearly}$$
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}2y&=2x+11\\y&=x+\frac{11}{2}\\[6pt]\text{This is a straight line with:}\\\text{slope }m&=1,\ \text{y-intercept }=\frac{11}{2}\\\text{Two points: }(0,\tfrac{11}{2}),\ (-\tfrac{11}{2},0)\\[8pt]y&=2x^2-3x-5\\\text{This is a parabola opening upwards}\\\text{Key points:}\\x&=0\Rightarrow y=-5\\x&=1\Rightarrow y=-6\\x&=2\Rightarrow y=-3\\\text{Plot these points and draw a smooth curve.}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.question_text: $$\text{Use your graph to find the coordinates of the points of intersection}$$
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.hint: $$\text{Points of intersection occur where the line and the curve cross}$$
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\text{From the graph, the line intersects the parabola at two points.}\\\text{Reading accurately from the graph:}\\\text{First intersection: }&(x,y)\approx(-2,\,3.5)\\\text{Second intersection: }&(x,y)\approx(1.5,\,7.0)\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.question_text: $$\text{Verify the intersection points by substitution into both equations}$$
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\textbf{Check }(-2,\,3.5):\\y&=x+\frac{11}{2}=-2+\frac{11}{2}=3.5\\y&=2(-2)^2-3(-2)-5=8+6-5=9\ \text{(not equal)}\\\text{Hence refine graph reading.}\\[6pt]\textbf{Exact solution (algebraic check):}\\x+\frac{11}{2}&=2x^2-3x-5\\2x^2-4x-\frac{21}{2}&=0\\4x^2-8x-21&=0\\x&=\frac{8\pm\sqrt{64+336}}{8}=\frac{8\pm20}{8}\\x&=3.5\ \text{or}\ -1.5\\[4pt]\textbf{Corresponding y-values:}\\x=3.5&:\ y=3.5+\frac{11}{2}=9\\x=-1.5&:\ y=-1.5+\frac{11}{2}=4\\[6pt]\therefore\ \text{Exact points of intersection are }&(3.5,\,9)\text{ and }(-1.5,\,4)\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.question_text: Use set notation to describe all $$x$$ such that $$3(x-2)>x-4$$ and $$4x+12>2x+17$$.
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.hint: Solve each inequality, then intersect the solutions.
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.correct_answer: From $$3x-6>x-4\Rightarrow2x>2\Rightarrow x>1$$ and $$4x+12>2x+17\Rightarrow2x>5\Rightarrow x>\tfrac{5}{2}$$; intersection: $$\{x\mid x>\tfrac{5}{2}\}=(\tfrac{5}{2},\infty).$$

Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.question_text: Use set notation to describe all $$x$$ such that $$2x-5<x-1$$ and $$7(x+1)>23-x$$.
Use set notation to describe all $$x$$ such that $$2x-3\ge2$$ and $$3(x+2)<12+x$$.
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.correct_answer: First $$2x\ge5\Rightarrow x\ge\tfrac{5}{2}$$; second $$3x+6<12+x\Rightarrow2x<6\Rightarrow x<3$$; intersection: $$\{x\mid \tfrac{5}{2}\le x<3\}=[\tfrac{5}{2},3).$$

Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.question_text: Use set notation to describe all $$x$$ such that $$15-x<2(11-x)$$ and $$5(3x-1)\ge12x+19$$.
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.correct_answer: First $$15-x<22-2x\Rightarrow x<7$$; second $$15x-5\ge12x+19\Rightarrow3x\ge24\Rightarrow x\ge8$$; intersection is $$\varnothing$$ (no real $$x$$).

Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.question_text: Use set notation to describe all $$x$$ such that $$3x+8\le20$$ and $$2(3x-7)\ge x+6$$.
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.correct_answer: First $$3x\le12\Rightarrow x\le4$$; second $$6x-14\ge x+6\Rightarrow5x\ge20\Rightarrow x\ge4$$; intersection: $$\{4\}.$$

Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.question_text: Use set notation to describe all $$x$$ such that $$5x+3<9$$ or $$5(2x+1)>27$$.
Use set notation to describe all $$x$$ such that $$4(3x+7)\le20$$ or $$2(3x-5)\ge\frac{7-6x}{2}$$.
Given $$A=\{x:3x+5>2\},\ B=\{x:\tfrac{x}{2}+1\le3\},\ C=\{x:11<2x-1\}$$ and $$A\cap(B\cup C)=\{x:p<x\le q\}\cup\{x:x>r\}$$, find $$p,q,r$$.
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.hint: Find each set, then compute $$B\cup C$$ and intersect with $$A$$.
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.correct_answer: $$A=(-1,\infty),\ B=(-\infty,4],\ C=(6,\infty)$$ so $$B\cup C=(-\infty,4]\cup(6,\infty).$$ Then $$A\cap(B\cup C)=(-1,4]\cup(6,\infty).$$ Hence $$p=-1,\ q=4,\ r=6.$$

Use set notation to describe $$x$$ such that $$x^2-x-6>0$$ and $$10-2x<5.$$
Use set notation to describe $$x$$ such that $$4x^2-3x-1<0$$ and $$4(x+2)<15-(x+7).$$
Use set notation to describe $$x$$ such that $$x^2-x-1<0$$ and $$14\le3x-2.$$

Find the set of values of x (x≠0) for which $$\frac{2}{x}<1.$$
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.hint: Multiply by x² and consider sign of x.
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.correct_answer: For x>0: 2<x ⇒ x>2; for x<0: 2>x ⇒ x<0; hence \boxed{x<0\text{ or }x>2}.

Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.question_text: Find the set of values of x (x≠0) for which $$5>\frac{4}{x}.$$
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.hint: Multiply both sides by x (consider sign).
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.correct_answer: For x>0: 5x>4⇒x>\tfrac45; for x<0: 5x<4⇒x<\tfrac45 (always true for x<0). Hence \boxed{x<0\text{ or }x>\tfrac45}.

Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.question_text: Find the set of values of x (x≠0) for which $$\frac{1}{x}+3>2.$$
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.correct_answer: For x>0: 1>-x ⇒ always true; for x<0: multiply gives 1<-x ⇒ x<-1. Hence \boxed{x>0\text{ or }x<-1}.

Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.question_text: Find the set of values of x (x≠0) for which $$6+\frac{5}{x}\ge\frac{8}{x}.$$
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.correct_answer: For x>0: 6x≥3⇒x≥\tfrac12; for x<0: 6x≤3⇒x≤\tfrac12 (always true for x<0). Hence \boxed{x<0\text{ or }x\ge\tfrac12}.

Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.hint: Use elimination: multiply first equation by 3 and add to second.

Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.question_text: Solve the equations $$x + 2y = 3$$ and $$x^2 - 4y^2 = -33.$$
Given $$x-2y=1$$ and $$3xy-y^2=8,$$ (a) Show that $$5y^2+3y-8=0.$$ (b) Find all pairs (x,y).
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.hint: Use substitution $$x=2y+1$$ into the second equation.

Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.question_text: By eliminating y from $$x+y=2$$ and $$x^2+xy-y^2=-1,$$ (a) show that $$x^2-6x+3=0$$. (b) Hence solve for x and y, giving results in the form $$a\pm b\sqrt6.$$
(a) Given that $$3^x = 9^{y-1},$$ show that $$x = 2y - 2.$$ (b) Solve the simultaneous equations $$x = 2y - 2$$ and $$x^2 = y^2 + 7.$$
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.hint: Use properties of indices and substitution.
Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.correct_answer: (a) $$9^{y-1}=(3^2)^{y-1}=3^{2y-2}\Rightarrow x=2y-2.$$ (b) Substitute into second: $$(2y-2)^2=y^2+7\Rightarrow3y^2-8y-3=0\Rightarrow y=3,-\tfrac13,$$ hence $$x=4,-\tfrac83.$$ \boxed{(x,y)=(4,3),(-\tfrac83,-\tfrac13)}.

Chapter 3 - Equations and inequal.question_text: (b) Solve the simultaneous equations $$x+2y=3$$ and $$x^2-2y+4y^2=18.$$

Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.question_text: Sketch the following curves and indicate clearly the points of intersection with the axes: $$y=(x-3)(x-2)(x+1)$$

Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.question_text: The graph of $$y=ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$$ is shown opposite, where $$a,b,c,d$$ are real constants. Find the values of $$a,b,c,d$$.
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.hint: Use factor form from x-intercepts (touching point is a repeated root), then use the y-intercept to find $$a$$.
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.correct_answer: $$x\text{-intercepts }-1,\ 3\text{ (double)}\Rightarrow y=a(x+1)(x-3)^2,\ y(0)=2\Rightarrow2=9a\Rightarrow a=\frac29,\ y=\frac29(x+1)(x-3)^2=\frac29x^3-\frac{10}9x^2+\frac23x+2\Rightarrow b=-\frac{10}9,\ c=\frac23,\ d=2$$

Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.question_text: Given that $$f(x)=(x-10)(x^2-2x)+12x$$ (a) Express $$f(x)$$ in the form $$x(ax^2+bx+c)$$ where $$a,b,c$$ are real constants. Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.correct_answer: $$\Delta=25-56=-31<0\Rightarrow x^2+5x+14\text{ has no real roots};\ y=0:\ x=-5,4;\ y(0)=5(-4)(14)=-280\Rightarrow(0,-280)$$

Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.question_text: $$\text{Use a separate diagram to sketch }y=\frac{2}{x^2}\text{ and }y=\frac{5}{x^2}.$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.hint: $$\text{For }y=\frac{k}{x^2}:\ x\ne0,\ \text{asymptotes }x=0,\ y=0,\ \text{symmetric about y-axis. If }k_2>k_1>0,\ \frac{k_2}{x^2}\text{ lies above }\frac{k_1}{x^2}.$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\textbf{Common features (both graphs):}\\\text{Domain: }&x\ne0\\\text{Vertical asymptote: }&x=0\\\text{Horizontal asymptote: }&y=0\\\text{Symmetry: }&y\text{-axis since }f(-x)=f(x)\\\text{Position: }&y>0\text{ (both above x-axis)}\\[6pt]\textbf{Key points to plot:}\\y=\frac{2}{x^2}:&(1,2),\ (2,\tfrac12),\ (-1,2),\ (-2,\tfrac12)\\y=\frac{5}{x^2}:&(1,5),\ (2,\tfrac54),\ (-1,5),\ (-2,\tfrac54)\\[6pt]\textbf{Relative position:}\\\frac{5}{x^2}&>\frac{2}{x^2}\ \text{for all }x\ne0\\\Rightarrow\ y=\frac{5}{x^2}&\text{ is always above }y=\frac{2}{x^2}.\\[6pt]\text{Draw two upward-opening reciprocal-squared branches in quadrants I and II approaching }x=0\text{ and }y=0,\ \text{and label each curve.}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.question_text: $$\text{Use a separate diagram to sketch }y=\frac{3}{x^2}\text{ and }y=-\frac{3}{x^2}.$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.hint: $$\text{Changing the sign reflects the graph in the x-axis. Both have asymptotes }x=0,\ y=0\text{ and are symmetric about the y-axis.}$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\textbf{Common features (both graphs):}\\\text{Domain: }&x\ne0\\\text{Vertical asymptote: }&x=0\\\text{Horizontal asymptote: }&y=0\\\text{Symmetry: }&y\text{-axis since }f(-x)=f(x)\\[6pt]\textbf{For }y=\frac{3}{x^2}:\\&k>0\Rightarrow y>0\text{ so branches are above the x-axis (quadrants I and II).}\\\text{Points: }&(1,3),\ (2,\tfrac34),\ (-1,3),\ (-2,\tfrac34)\\[6pt]\textbf{For }y=-\frac{3}{x^2}:\\&k<0\Rightarrow y<0\text{ so branches are below the x-axis (quadrants III and IV).}\\&\text{This is the reflection of }y=\frac{3}{x^2}\text{ in the x-axis.}\\\text{Points: }&(1,-3),\ (2,-\tfrac34),\ (-1,-3),\ (-2,-\tfrac34)\\[6pt]\text{Sketch both sets of branches approaching }x=0\text{ and }y=0,\ \text{and label each curve clearly.}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.question_text: $$\text{Use a separate diagram to sketch }y=-\frac{2}{x^2}\text{ and }y=-\frac{6}{x^2}.$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.hint: $$\text{Both have }k<0\Rightarrow\text{ both curves lie below the x-axis; larger }|k|\text{ gives values further down (more negative).}$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\textbf{Common features (both graphs):}\\\text{Domain: }&x\ne0\\\text{Vertical asymptote: }&x=0\\\text{Horizontal asymptote: }&y=0\\\text{Symmetry: }&y\text{-axis since }f(-x)=f(x)\\\text{Position: }&y<0\text{ (both below x-axis, in quadrants III and IV)}\\[6pt]\textbf{Key points to plot:}\\y=-\frac{2}{x^2}:&(1,-2),\ (2,-\tfrac12),\ (-1,-2),\ (-2,-\tfrac12)\\y=-\frac{6}{x^2}:&(1,-6),\ (2,-\tfrac32),\ (-1,-6),\ (-2,-\tfrac32)\\[6pt]\textbf{Relative position:}\\-\frac{6}{x^2}&<-\frac{2}{x^2}\ \text{for all }x\ne0\\\Rightarrow\ y=-\frac{6}{x^2}&\text{ lies below }y=-\frac{2}{x^2}\text{ everywhere.}\\[6pt]\text{Draw two downward reciprocal-squared branches in quadrants III and IV approaching }x=0\text{ and }y=0,\ \text{and label each curve.}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.question_text: $$\text{(a) On the same axes sketch the curves }y=(x+1)^3\text{ and }y=3x(x-1).\ \text{(b) Explain how your sketch shows that there is only one real solution to }x^3+6x+1=0.$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.hint: $$\text{At intersection points }(x+1)^3=3x(x-1).\ \text{The number of real solutions equals the number of intersections.}$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\textbf{Curve }y=(x+1)^3:&\ \text{increasing cubic for all }x\\\text{x-intercept: }(x+1)^3=0&\Rightarrow x=-1\\\text{y-intercept: }x=0&\Rightarrow y=1\\[6pt]\textbf{Curve }y=3x(x-1):&=3x^2-3x\ \text{(upward parabola)}\\\text{x-intercepts: }&x=0,\ 1\\\text{Vertex: }&x=\tfrac12,\ y=-\tfrac34\\[8pt]\textbf{Intersections:}\\(x+1)^3&=3x(x-1)\\x^3+3x^2+3x+1&=3x^2-3x\\x^3+6x+1&=0\\[6pt]\text{From the sketch, the graphs intersect once only.}\\\therefore\ \text{the equation has exactly one real solution.}\end{aligned}$$
$$f(x)=x^2-x^3,\ x^2(1-x)=0\Rightarrow x=0\text{ (double root)},1;\ y\text{-intercept }(0,0);\ \text{cubic touching x-axis at }(0,0)\text{ and crossing at }(1,0).$$
$$y=f(x+1)\text{ is the graph of }y=f(x)\text{ shifted }1\text{ unit to the left.}$$

Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.question_text: $$\text{Sketch the curve }y=x^2+3x-4.$$ $$\text{On the same axes, sketch the graph of }5y=x^2+3x-4.$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.hint: $$5y=x^2+3x-4\Rightarrow y=\tfrac15(x^2+3x-4)\text{ is a vertical scale factor } \tfrac15\text{ of }y=x^2+3x-4.$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.correct_answer: $$y=\tfrac15(x^2+3x-4);\ \text{x-intercepts unchanged: }(-4,0),(1,0);\ \text{y-intercept: }(0,-\tfrac45);\ \text{vertex: }\left(-\tfrac32,-\tfrac54\right);\ \text{same axis of symmetry }x=-\tfrac32,\ \text{opens upward, flatter than (a).}$$

Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.question_text: $$\text{The point }P(2,1)\text{ lies on }y=f(x).\ \text{On the graph of }y=af(x),\ P\text{ maps to }Q(4,1).\ \text{Determine }a.$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.hint: $$\text{For }y=af(x),\ x\text{ stays the same and }y\text{ is multiplied by }a.$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.correct_answer: $$\text{Under }y=af(x),\ (x,y)\mapsto(x,ay).\ \text{So }P(2,1)\mapsto(2,a).\ \text{Given image is }Q(4,1)\text{ (same y as original), this indicates a horizontal stretch by factor }2\text{, i.e. }y=f\!\left(\tfrac{x}{2}\right).\ \text{But if the intended transformation is }y=af(x)\text{ then }x\text{ cannot change, so the only consistent value is }a=1.$$

Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.question_title: Image of P under given transformations
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.question_text: $$\text{Write down the coordinates of the point to which }P(2,1)\text{ maps under: (i) }f(x-4)\ \text{(ii) }3f(x)\ \text{(iii) }\tfrac15 f(x)-4.$$
$$\text{The diagram shows the curve }y=5+2x-x^2\text{ and the line }y=2.\ \text{The curve and the line intersect at points }A\text{ and }B.\ \text{Find the x-coordinates of }A\text{ and }B.$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.hint: $$\text{At points of intersection, set the equations equal: }5+2x-x^2=2.$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}5+2x-x^2&=2\\-x^2+2x+3&=0\\x^2-2x-3&=0\\(x-3)(x+1)&=0\\x&=3\ \text{or}\ x=-1\\\therefore\ \text{The x-coordinates of }A\text{ and }B\text{ are }-1\text{ and }3.\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: The line joining (3,-5) to (6,a) has gradient 4. Work out $$a.$$
The line joining (5,b) to (8,3) has gradient -3. Work out $$b.$$
The line joining (c,4) to (7,6) has gradient $$\frac34.$$
The line joining (-1,2d) to (1,4) has gradient $$-\frac14.$$
The line joining (-3,-2) to (2e,5) has gradient 2. Work out $$e.$$
The line joining (7,2) to (f,3f) has gradient 4. Find $$f.$$
The line joining (3,-4) to (-g,2g) has gradient -3. Work out $$g.$$
Show that the points $$A(2,3), B(4,4)$$ and $$C(10,7)$$ can be joined by a straight line.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Find gradient of $$AB$$ and $$AC$$; if equal, points are collinear.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: $$m_{AB}=\frac{4-3}{4-2}=\frac12, \quad m_{AC}=\frac{7-3}{10-2}=\frac12.$$ Since $$m_{AB}=m_{AC},$$ all three points lie on the same line.

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: Show that the points $$A(-2a,5a), B(0,4a)$$ and $$C(6a,a)$$ are collinear.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Compare gradients $$m_{AB}$$ and $$m_{BC}.$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: $$m_{AB}=\frac{4a-5a}{0-(-2a)}=-\frac12, \quad m_{BC}=\frac{a-4a}{6a-0}=-\frac12.$$ Thus $$m_{AB}=m_{BC},$$ so the three points are collinear.

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Use $$m=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}.$$ Then use $$y-y_1=m(x-x_1).$$

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: The line $$l_1:y=3x-7$$ intersects $$l_2:y+4x-17=0$$ at P(-3,b). (a) Find $$b.$$ (b) Find $$a.$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Substitute $$x=-3$$ into both lines, equate $$y$$ to find $$b$$. Then use $$l_2$$ form to find $$a$$ if needed.

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: Vertices of triangle ABC are A(3,5), B(-2,0), C(4,-1). Find equations of the sides AB, BC, CA.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Find gradient for each pair and use $$y-y_1=m(x-x_1).$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: $$AB: m=1\Rightarrow y=x+2.$$ $$BC: m=-\tfrac15\Rightarrow y=-\tfrac15x-\tfrac25.$$ $$CA: m=-3\Rightarrow y=-3x+14.$$

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: The straight line $$l$$ passes through $$(a,4)$$ and $$(3a,3).$$ An equation of $$l$$ is $$x+6y+c=0.$$ Find the values of $$a$$ and $$c.$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Substitute both points into $$x+6y+c=0$$ to form two equations, then eliminate $$c$$ to find $$a.$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: For $$(a,4): a+24+c=0$$ and $$(3a,3): 3a+18+c=0.$$ Subtract → $$2a-6=0\Rightarrow a=3.$$ Substitute $$a=3$$ → $$3+24+c=0\Rightarrow c=-27.$$ Hence $$a=3, c=-27.$$

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: The line $$y=4x-8$$ meets the x-axis at $$A$$. Find the equation of the line with gradient $$3$$ passing through $$A$$.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Set $$y=0$$ to find $$A$$, then use $$y-y_1=m(x-x_1).$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: At $$y=0$$: $$0=4x-8\Rightarrow x=2,$$ so $$A(2,0).$$ Then $$y-0=3(x-2)\Rightarrow y=3x-6.$$ Hence $$y=3x-6.$$

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: The line $$y=-2x+8$$ meets the y-axis at $$B$$. Find the equation of the line with gradient $$2$$ through $$B$$.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: On y-axis, $$x=0.$$ Then use $$y-y_1=m(x-x_1).$$

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Set $$y=0$$ to find $$C,$$ then use point-slope form.

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Find $$B(0,2)$$ then use gradient formula $$m=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}.$$

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: The line $$y=4x+5$$ meets y-axis at $$C$$, and $$y=-3x-15$$ meets x-axis at $$D$$. Find the equation of line joining $$C$$ and $$D$$ in $$ax+by+c=0$$ form.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Find $$C(0,5)$$ and $$D(-5,0),$$ then use gradient formula.

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: Lines $$y=x-5$$ and $$y=3x-13$$ intersect at $$S$$. Point $$T(-4,2)$$. Find equation of line through $$S$$ and $$T$$.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Find $$S$$ by solving equations, then use two-point form.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: At intersection: $$x-5=3x-13\Rightarrow x=4,y=-1\Rightarrow S(4,-1).$$ Gradient $$m=\frac{2+1}{-4-4}=-\frac{3}{8}.$$ Equation: $$y+1=-\frac{3}{8}(x-4)\Rightarrow3x+8y-4=0.$$

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: Lines $$y=-2x+1$$ and $$y=x+7$$ intersect at $$L$$. Point $$M(-3,1).$$ Find equation of line joining $$L$$ and $$M$$.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Find $$L$$ by solving equations, then use gradient formula.

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: Work out whether each pair of lines is parallel:a) $$y=5x-2$$ and $$15x-3y+9=0$$, b) $$7x+14y-1=0$$ and $$y=\frac12x+9$$, c) $$4x-3y-8=0$$ and $$3x-4y-8=0$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Find gradients of each and compare — parallel lines have equal gradients.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: (a) Gradients $$5$$ and $$5$$ → parallel. (b) Gradients $$-\frac12$$ and $$\frac12$$ → not parallel. (c) Gradients $$\frac43$$ and $$\frac34$$ → not parallel.

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: The lines \(y=5x-3\) and \(5x-y+4=0\).
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Rearrange second to \(y=5x+4\); both have same gradient \(m=5\).

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Rearrange first to \(y=5x-1\); product of gradients \(5\times(-\tfrac{1}{5})=-1\).

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Rearrange second to \(y=\tfrac{2}{3}x-3\); gradients \(-\tfrac{3}{2}\) and \(\tfrac{2}{3}\) → product = -1.
Divide 2nd by 2 → same form as 1st → identical gradients → parallel.
Gradients \(-\tfrac{3}{2}\) and \(-\tfrac{2}{3}\); product \(=\tfrac{6}{6}=1\neq-1\).
Gradients \(m_1=5, m_2=-\tfrac{1}{5}\); product = -1 → perpendicular.

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: Find the equation of the line passing through (-2,-3) and perpendicular to $$y=\frac{4}{7}x+5.$$ Write in form $$ax+by+c=0$$ where a,b,c are integers.

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: Line $$l$$ passes through (-3,0) and (3,-2); line $$n$$ passes through (1,8) and (-1,2). Show $$l$$ and $$n$$ are perpendicular.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Find gradients and show their product = -1.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: $$m_l=\frac{-2-0}{3-(-3)}=-\frac13,\; m_n=\frac{2-8}{-1-1}=3\Rightarrow m_lm_n=-1.$$ Therefore, lines $$l$$ and $$n$$ are perpendicular.

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: Quadrilateral $$ABCD$$ with $$A(-1,5), B(7,1), C(5,-3), D(-3,1).$$ Show it is a rectangle.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Find gradients of all sides and show adjacent sides are perpendicular.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: $$m_{AB}=\frac{1-5}{7+1}=-\frac12,\; m_{BC}=\frac{-3-1}{5-7}=2.$$ $$m_{CD}=\frac{1+3}{-3-5}=-\frac12,\; m_{DA}=\frac{5-1}{-1+3}=2.$$ Opposite sides parallel, adjacent sides perpendicular ⇒ rectangle.

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: A line $$l_1: 5x+11y-7=0$$ crosses x-axis at A. Line $$l_2$$ is perpendicular to $$l_1$$ and passes through A. Find:  (a) Coordinates of A (b) Equation of $$l_2$$ in $$ax+by+c=0$$ form.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Find A by setting y=0, then find perpendicular slope = negative reciprocal of slope of $$l_1$$.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: (a) When $$ y=0 \Rightarrow 5x-7=0 \Rightarrow A(7/5,0)$$.(b) $$l_1: 5x+11y-7=0 \Rightarrow y=-\frac{5}{11}x+\frac{7}{11}$$ → slope = -5/11, perpendicular slope = 11/5.$$y-0=\frac{11}{5}(x-\frac{7}{5})\Rightarrow5y=11x-77/5\Rightarrow55x-25y-77=0.$$

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: The vertices of a triangle are A(2,7), B(5,–6), C(8,–6). (a) Show triangle is scalene. (b) Find area of triangle ABC.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Scalene triangles have three unequal sides. We know that, Area = ½×base×height.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: a) Sides: AB=√(3²+13²)=√178, BC=3, AC=√(6²+13²)=√205 → all different. b) Area = ½×3×13=19.5.

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: The straight line \(l_1\) has equation \(y=7x-3\). The straight line \(l_2\) has equation \(4x+3y-41=0\). The lines intersect at the point \(A\). (a) Work out the coordinates of \(A\). (b) The straight line \(l_2\) crosses the \(x\)-axis at the point \(B\). Work out the coordinates of \(B\). (c) Work out the area of triangle \(AOB\).
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Solve \(7x-3=\frac{41-4x}{3}\) for \(A\); set \(y=0\) in \(l_2\) for \(B\); use triangle area \(\tfrac12|x_Ay_B-y_Ax_B|\).

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: The straight line \(l_1\) has equation \(4x-5y-10=0\) and intersects the \(x\)-axis at point \(A\). The straight line \(l_2\) has equation \(4x-2y+20=0\) and intersects the \(x\)-axis at point \(B\). (a) Find \(A\). (b) Find \(B\). The lines \(l_1\) and \(l_2\) intersect at point \(C\). (c) Find \(C\). (d) Work out the area of triangle \(ABC\).
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Set \(y=0\) to get \(x\)-intercepts; solve the two-line system for \(C\); for area use shoelace or \(\tfrac12\cdot\text{base}\cdot\text{height}\).

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: The straight line $$l_1$$ passes through $$(-4,14)$$ with gradient $$-\tfrac14$$. (a) Find its equation in the form $$ax+by+c=0$$. (b) Find where it crosses the y-axis (A). The line $$l_2$$ passes through the origin with gradient 3. The lines intersect at B. (c) Find coordinates of B. (d) Find the exact area of $$\triangle OAB$$.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Use point–slope form $$y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$$ to get $$l_1$$, then set $$x=0$$ for A, solve simultaneously for B, then area formula $$\tfrac12|x_Ay_B-y_Ax_B|.$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: (a) $$y-14=-\tfrac14(x+4)\Rightarrow y=-\tfrac14x+13$$ → $$x+4y-52=0.$$ (b) At $$x=0,$$ $$y=13$$ → $$A(0,13).$$ (c) For $$l_2:y=3x,$$ solve $$3x=-\tfrac14x+13\Rightarrow 13=\tfrac{13x}{4}\Rightarrow x=4,\ y=12\Rightarrow B(4,12).$$ (d) $$\text{Area}=\tfrac12|0\cdot12-13\cdot4|=\tfrac12(52)=26.$$

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: A website designer charges a flat fee and a daily rate. Company A’s site takes 6 days and costs £7100; Company B’s takes 13 days and costs £9550. (a) Write an equation linking days $$d$$ and cost $$C$$ in the form $$C=ad+b$$. (b) Interpret $$a$$ and $$b$$. (c) If a third company is charged £13 400, find the number of days.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Set up two points $$(d,C)=(6,7100),(13,9550)$$ and fit $$C=ad+b$$.

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: The average August temperature in Exeter is $$20^\circ\text{C}$$ or $$68^\circ\text{F}$$; the average January temperature is $$9^\circ\text{C}$$ or $$48.2^\circ\text{F}$$. (a) Find a linear equation linking Fahrenheit $$F$$ and Celsius $$C$$ in the form $$F=aC+b$$. (b) Interpret $$a,b$$. (c) Convert the UK record of $$101.3^\circ\text{F}$$ to Celsius. (d) For what value is the temperature the same in both scales?
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Use the two points $$(C,F)=(20,68),(9,48.2)$$ to determine $$a,b$$; then invert to convert; solve $$F=C$$.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: (a) $$a=\dfrac{68-48.2}{20-9}=1.8=\tfrac{9}{5},\ b=68-1.8\cdot20=32\Rightarrow F=\tfrac{9}{5}C+32.$$ (b) $$a=\tfrac{9}{5}$$ is the scale factor; $$b=32$$ is the offset (freezing point). (c) $$C=\dfrac{101.3-32}{1.8}=38.5^\circ\text{C}.$$ (d) $$C=F\Rightarrow C=1.8C+32\Rightarrow C=-40,$$ so $$-40^\circ$$ on both scales.

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: In 2004 a city had 17 500 homes with internet connections. A service provider predicts an additional 750 homes will get internet each year after 2004. (a) Write a linear model for the number of homes $$n$$ with internet connections $$t$$ years after 2004. (b) State one assumption of this model.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Model linear growth from initial value.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: (a) $$n=17500+750t.$$ (b) Assumes the increase is constant at 750 homes per year (linear growth) and other factors remain unchanged.

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: The points $$A(2,16)$$ and $$B(12,-4)$$ have coordinates as shown. A straight line $$l_1$$ passes through $$A$$ and $$B$$. (a) Find an equation for $$l_1$$ in the form $$ax+by=c.$$ The line $$l_2$$ passes through the point $$C(-1,1)$$ and has gradient $$\tfrac{1}{3}.$$ (b) Find an equation for $$l_2.$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Use gradient between $$A$$ and $$B$$, apply point–slope form, and rearrange to $$ax+by=c.$$

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: The points $$A(-1,-2),\ B(7,2),\ C(k,4)$$ are the vertices of $$\triangle ABC$$, where angle $$ABC$$ is a right angle. (a) Find the gradient of $$AB$$. (b) Calculate the value of $$k$$. (c) Find an equation of the straight line passing through $$B$$ and $$C$$ in the form $$ax+by+c=0$$. (d) Calculate the area of $$\triangle ABC.$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Use gradient formula for perpendicular lines and right-angle condition $$m_{AB}\times m_{BC}=-1.$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: (a) $$m_{AB}=\tfrac{2-(-2)}{7-(-1)}=\tfrac{4}{8}=\tfrac{1}{2}.$$ (b) For right angle at $$B,$$ $$m_{AB}\cdot m_{BC}=-1\Rightarrow\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot m_{BC}=-1\Rightarrow m_{BC}=-2.$$ Using $$B(7,2)$$ and $$C(k,4):4-2=-2(k-7)\Rightarrow k=8.$$ (c) $$m_{BC}=-2,\ y-2=-2(x-7)\Rightarrow2x+y-16=0.$$ (d) Base $$AB=8\sqrt{1^2+(0.5)^2}=\sqrt{80}=8.94,$$ height $$=|4-2|=2,$$ so $$\text{Area}=\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot8\cdot4=16.$$

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: Find an equation of the straight line passing through the points with coordinates $$(-1,5)$$ and $$(4,-2)$$, giving your answer in the form $$ax+by+c=0$$, where $$a,b,c$$ are integers. The line crosses the x-axis at point $$A$$ and the y-axis at point $$B$$, and $$O$$ is the origin. (a) Find an equation of the line. (b) Find the area of $$\triangle AOB.$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Find gradient and use two-point form, then use intercepts to calculate area with coordinate formula.

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: The straight line $$l_1$$ has equation $$4y+x=0.$$ The straight line $$l_2$$ has equation $$y=2x-3.$$ (a) On the same axes, sketch both lines showing coordinates of intercepts. (b) The lines $$l_1$$ and $$l_2$$ intersect at point $$A$$. Calculate exact fractions for $$A$$. (c) Find an equation of the line through $$A$$ which is perpendicular to $$l_1$$, in the form $$ax+by+c=0.$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Use intercepts, substitution, and perpendicular slope relation $$m_1m_2=-1.$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: (a) For $$l_1:4y+x=0\Rightarrow y=-\tfrac{1}{4}x$$ (passes through $$(0,0)$$ and $$(4,-1)$$). For $$l_2:y=2x-3$$ (intercepts $$(0,-3)$$ and $$(\tfrac{3}{2},0)$$). (b) Intersection: $$-\tfrac{1}{4}x=2x-3\Rightarrow9x=12\Rightarrow x=\tfrac{4}{3},y=-\tfrac{1}{3}\Rightarrow A(\tfrac{4}{3},-\tfrac{1}{3}).$$ (c) $$m_{l_1}=-\tfrac{1}{4}\Rightarrow m_\perp=4.$$ Equation through $$A: y+\tfrac{1}{3}=4(x-\tfrac{4}{3})\Rightarrow4x-y-\tfrac{17}{3}=0\Rightarrow12x-3y-17=0.$$

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: The points $$A(4,6)$$ and $$B(12,2)$$ are given. The straight line $$l_1$$ passes through $$A$$ and $$B.$$ (a) Find the equation of $$l_1$$ in the form $$ax+by+c=0.$$ The straight line $$l_2$$ passes through the origin and has gradient $$-\tfrac{2}{3}.$$ (b) Write down an equation for $$l_2.$$ The lines $$l_1$$ and $$l_2$$ intersect at point $$C.$$ (c) Find the coordinates of $$C.$$ (d) Show that lines $$OA$$ and $$OC$$ are perpendicular, where $$O$$ is the origin. (e) Work out the lengths of $$OA$$ and $$OC$$ in the form $$k\sqrt{13}.$$ (f) Hence calculate the area of $$\triangle OAC.$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Use two-point form for $$l_1$$, solve for intersection, then apply perpendicularity and distance formula.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: (a) $$m=\tfrac{2-6}{12-4}=-\tfrac{1}{2},\ y-6=-\tfrac{1}{2}(x-4)\Rightarrow x+2y-16=0.$$ (b) $$y=-\tfrac{2}{3}x.$$ (c) Solve $$x+2(-\tfrac{2}{3}x)-16=0\Rightarrow -\tfrac{1}{3}x=16\Rightarrow x=-48,\ y=32\Rightarrow C(-48,32).$$ (d) $$m_{OA}=\tfrac{6-0}{4-0}=\tfrac{3}{2},\ m_{OC}=\tfrac{32-0}{-48-0}=-\tfrac{2}{3},\ m_{OA}m_{OC}=-1\Rightarrow\text{perpendicular.}$$ (e) $$OA=\sqrt{4^2+6^2}=\sqrt{52}=2\sqrt{13},\ OC=\sqrt{(-48)^2+32^2}=\sqrt{64\times52}=8\sqrt{13}.$$ (f) $$\text{Area}=\tfrac{1}{2}(OA\times OC)=\tfrac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{13}\times8\sqrt{13})=104.$$

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: Point $$A$$ is $$(-1,5).$$ Let $$(x,y)$$ be any point on the line $$y=3x.$$ (a) Write an equation in terms of $$x$$ for the distance between $$(x,y)$$ and $$A(-1,5).$$ (b) Find coordinates of the two points $$B$$ and $$C$$ on the line $$y=3x$$ that are a distance of $$\sqrt{74}$$ from $$(-1,5).$$ (c) Find the equation of the line $$l_1$$ perpendicular to $$y=3x$$ and passing through $$(-1,5).$$ (d) Find the coordinates of the intersection of $$l_1$$ and $$y=3x.$$ (e) Find the area of $$\triangle ABC.$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Use distance formula, substitution, perpendicular slope relation, and area formula.

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: Find the area of the triangle with vertices $$A(-2,-2),\ B(13,8),\ C(-4,14).$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Use coordinate area formula $$\text{Area}=\tfrac12|x_1(y_2-y_3)+x_2(y_3-y_1)+x_3(y_1-y_2)|.$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The line segment $$FG$$ is a diameter of a circle centre $$C(6,1).$$ Given $$F(2,-3),$$ find $$G.$$
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Use midpoint relation $$6=\tfrac{2+x_G}{2},1=\tfrac{-3+y_G}{2}.$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The line segment $$CD$$ is a diameter of a circle centre $$(-2a,5a).$$ Given $$D(3a,-7a),$$ find $$C.$$
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Use midpoint formula backward.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: $$(-2a,5a)=\!\left(\tfrac{C_x+3a}{2},\tfrac{C_y-7a}{2}\right)\!\Rightarrow C(-7a,17a).$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: Points $$M(3,p),N(4,q)$$ lie on a circle centre $$(5,6).$$ The diameter $$MN$$ has midpoint $$(5,6).$$ Find $$p,q.$$
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Set midpoint conditions $$\tfrac{3+4}{2}=5,\ \tfrac{p+q}{2}=6.$$
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: $$p+q=12\Rightarrow(p,q)=(4,8)\text{ or any satisfying sum 12.}$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: Point $$X(7,-2)$$ and point $$Y(4,q)$$. The perpendicular bisector of $$XY$$ has equation $$y=4x+b$$. Find the values of $$q$$ and $$b$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Use slope condition $$m_\perp\cdot m_{XY}=-1$$ and midpoint lies on bisector.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: From $$m_\perp=4$$, $$m_{XY}=-\tfrac14=\tfrac{q+2}{4-7}=-\tfrac{q+2}{3}\Rightarrow q=-\tfrac54.$$ Midpoint $$M(\tfrac{7+4}{2},\tfrac{-2+q}{2})=(\tfrac{11}{2},-\tfrac{13}{8}).$$ On $$y=4x+b$$: $$-\tfrac{13}{8}=4\cdot\tfrac{11}{2}+b\Rightarrow b=-\tfrac{189}{8}.$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: Triangle $$PQR$$ has vertices $$P(6,9),Q(3,-3),R(-9,3).$$ (a) Find the perpendicular bisectors of each side of the triangle. (b) Show that all three perpendicular bisectors meet at a single point and find its coordinates.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Midpoints and perpendicular slopes for $$PQ,QR,PR$$; write their equations and solve any two to get the circumcenter.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: $$\text{Bisector of }PQ:\ 2x+8y-33=0;\quad \text{of }QR:\ 2x-y+6=0;\quad \text{of }PR:\ 10x+4y-9=0.$$ Solving (first two): $$x=-\tfrac{5}{6},\ y=\tfrac{13}{3}.$$ Substituting into the third satisfies it, so all three concur at $$\big(-\tfrac{5}{6},\tfrac{13}{3}\big).$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: A circle $$C$$ has equation $$x^2+y^2+12x+2y=k,$$ where $$k$$ is constant. (a) Find centre of $$C.$$ (b) State range of possible values of $$k.$$
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Complete the square in $$x,y$$.

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The point $$P(7,-14)$$ lies on the circle $$x^2+y^2+6x-14y=17$$. The point $$Q$$ also lies on the circle such that $$PQ$$ is a diameter. Find coordinates of $$Q.$$
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Find centre via completing squares, then use midpoint condition $$\text{Mid}(P,Q)=\text{centre}$$.

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The circle with equation $$(x-k)^2+y^2=41$$ passes through $$(3,4)$$. Find two possible values of $$k.$$
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Substitute point and solve for $$k$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: $$(3-k)^2+4^2=41\Rightarrow(3-k)^2=25\Rightarrow3-k=\pm5\Rightarrow k=-2\text{ or }8.$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: A circle with equation $$(x-k)^2+(y-2)^2=50$$ passes through the point $$(4,-5).$$ Find the possible values of $$k$$ and the equation of each circle.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Substitute the point and solve for $$k$$; then write both circle equations.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: Hence, $$(x-k)^2+(y-2)^2=50$$ passes through the point $$(4,-5)$$. Put the value of the x, y in equation, $$(4-k)^2+(-5-2)^2=50\Rightarrow(4-k)^2+49=50\Rightarrow(4-k)^2=1.$$ Hence $$4-k=\pm1\Rightarrow k=3\ \text{or}\ k=5.$$ Therefore the two circles are $$\boxed{(x-3)^2+(y-2)^2=50}$$ and $$\boxed{(x-5)^2+(y-2)^2=50}$$ (same radius, centres at $$(3,2)$$ and $$(5,2)$$, both 1 unit horizontally from the point’s perpendicular through the centre).

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: By completing the square for $$x$$ and $$y$$, show that the equation $$x^2+y^2+2fx+2gy+c=0$$ describes a circle with centre $$(-f,-g)$$ and radius $$\sqrt{f^2+g^2-c}.$$
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Rearrange and complete the square in each variable.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: Group: $$(x^2+2fx)+(y^2+2gy)+c=0.$$ Complete squares: $$(x+f)^2-f^2+(y+g)^2-g^2+c=0\Rightarrow (x+f)^2+(y+g)^2=f^2+g^2-c.$$ Hence the centre is $$(-f,-g)$$ and $$r^2=f^2+g^2-c$$ (so a real circle requires $$f^2+g^2-c>0$$).

Chapter 6 - Circles.subtopic_name: Intersections of straight lines and circles
Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The circle with equation $$(x-4)^2+(y+7)^2=50$$ meets the line $$x-y-5=0$$ at $$A,B$$. (a) Find the coordinates of of the points $$A,B$$. (b) Find the equation perpendicular bisector of line segment $$AB$$. (c) Show this bisector of AB passes through the circle’s centre. (d) Find the area of $$\triangle OAB$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Use $$y=x-5$$ in the circle; midpoint–slope for bisector; check centre; area with base–height.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: (a) Substitute: $$(x-4)^2+(x+2)^2=50\Rightarrow2x^2-4x-30=0\Rightarrow x=5,-3.$$ Then $$y=x-5\Rightarrow A(5,0),\ B(-3,-8).$$ (b) $$M=\big(\tfrac{5+(-3)}{2},\tfrac{0+(-8)}{2}\big)=(1,-4),\ m_{AB}=1\Rightarrow m_\perp=-1,$$ so $$y+4=-1(x-1)\Rightarrow x+y+3=0.$$ (c) Centre $$C(4,-7):\ 4+(-7)+3=0\Rightarrow C$$ lies on the bisector. (d) Base $$OA=5$$ on the $$x$$-axis, height $$=|y_B|=8,$$ so $$\text{Area}=\tfrac12\cdot5\cdot8=\boxed{20}.$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.subtopic_name: Intersections of straight lines and circles
Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The line $$y=kx$$ intersects the circle $$x^2-10x+y^2-12y+57=0$$ at two distinct points. (a) Show that $$21k^2-60k+32<0.$$ (b) Hence find the range of the possible value of  $$k$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Substitute $$y=kx$$ and require discriminant $$>0$$.

Chapter 6 - Circles.subtopic_name: Intersections of straight lines and circles
Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The line $$y=4x-1$$ does not intersect the circle $$x^2+2x+y^2=k$$. Find the range of possible values of $$k$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Substitute and set discriminant $$<0$$; also require a real circle.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: $$x^2+2x+(4x-1)^2=k\Rightarrow 17x^2-6x+1-k=0.$$ $$\Delta=(-6)^2-4\cdot17(1-k)<0\Rightarrow36-68(1-k)<0\Rightarrow k<\tfrac{8}{17}.$$ Since a circle needs $$k>-1$$ (because $$(x+1)^2+y^2=k+1$$), range $$\boxed{-1<k<\tfrac{8}{17}}.$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.subtopic_name: Intersections of straight lines and circles
Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The line $$y=2x+5$$ meets the circle $$x^2+kx+y^2=4$$ at exactly one point. Find the two possible values of $$k$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Substitute and set discriminant $$=0$$.

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The Circle has the equation $$ x^2+18x+y^2-2y+29=0.$$ (a) Verify $$P(-7,-6)$$ lies on $$C$$. (b) Find an equation of the tangent to $$C$$ at $$P$$ in the form $$y=mx+b$$. (c) Find the coordinates of $$R,$$ the intersection of this tangent with the $$y$$-axis. (d) Find the area of $$\triangle APR,$$ where $$A$$ is the centre of $$C$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Complete squares for centre; use radius–tangent perpendicularity; for (d) use area $$\tfrac12|x_A(y_P-y_R)+x_P(y_R-y_A)+x_R(y_A-y_P)|$$ or vector determinant.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: (a) $$49-126+36+12+29=0\Rightarrow P\in C.$$ (b) $$(x+9)^2+(y-1)^2=53\Rightarrow A(-9,1).$$ Radius slope $$=\tfrac{-6-1}{-7-(-9)}=-\tfrac72\Rightarrow m_t=\tfrac{2}{7}.$$ Tangent: $$y+6=\tfrac{2}{7}(x+7)\Rightarrow \boxed{y=\tfrac{2}{7}x-4}.$$ (c) Set $$x=0\Rightarrow R(0,-4).$$ (d) $$A(-9,1),P(-7,-6),R(0,-4).$$ Area $$=\tfrac12|\,\det(\overrightarrow{AP},\overrightarrow{AR})\,|=\tfrac12|\,\langle2,-7\rangle\times\langle9,-5\rangle\,|=\tfrac12|(-10+63)|=\boxed{\tfrac{53}{2}}.$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The tangent to the circle $$(x+4)^2+(y-1)^2=242$$ at $$(7,-10)$$ meets the $$y$$-axis at $$S$$ and the $$x$$-axis at $$T$$. (a) Find $$S,T$$. (b) Hence find the area of $$\triangle OST$$ where $$O$$ is the origin.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Find tangent eqn using point–radius perpendicularity, then find intercepts.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: (a) Centre $$(-4,1)$$; radius slope $$=\tfrac{-10-1}{7+4}=-1.$$ Hence tangent slope $$=1$$. Through $$(7,-10): y+10=1(x-7)\Rightarrow y=x-17.$$ For $$S$$: $$x=0\Rightarrow y=-17\Rightarrow S(0,-17);$$ for $$T$$: $$y=0\Rightarrow x=17\Rightarrow T(17,0).$$ (b) Area $$=\tfrac12|x_Ty_S-x_Sy_T|=\tfrac12(17\times17)=\boxed{144.5}.$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The circle $$C$$ has centre $$P(11,-5)$$ and passes through $$Q(5,3)$$. (a) Find the equation of $$C$$. (b) The line $$l_1$$ is tangent to $$C$$ at $$Q$$ — find its equation. (c) The line $$l_2$$ is parallel to $$l_1$$ and passes through the midpoint of $$PQ$$; it meets $$C$$ at $$A,B$$. Find the coordinates of $$A,B$$. (d) Find the length $$AB$$ in simplest surd form.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Use distance formula for radius; tangent ⟂ radius; parallel line through midpoint; intersection via substitution; distance formula for $$AB$$.

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_title: Circle from two points (line through centre)
Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The points $$R(2,3)$$ and $$S(10,1)$$ lie on a circle with centre $$C(a,-2)$$. Let $$M$$ be the midpoint of $$RS$$. The line $$l$$ passes through $$M$$ and $$C$$. (a) Find an equation of $$l$$. (b) Find the value of $$a$$. (c) Find the equation of the circle. (d) Find the points of intersection, $$A$$ and $$B$$, of the line $$l$$ and the circle.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Use midpoint for $$M$$; slope of $$MC$$ for $$l$$; set $$CR=CS$$ to get $$a$$; circle $$(x-a)^2+(y+2)^2=r^2$$ with $$r^2=CR^2$$; substitute $$l$$ into circle for $$A,B$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: (a) $$M(6,2),\ C(a,-2)\Rightarrow m=\dfrac{-2-2}{a-6}=\dfrac{-4}{a-6};\ \text{with }a=5\Rightarrow m=4,\ l:\ y-2=4(x-6)\iff y=4x-22.$$ (b) $$CR^2=CS^2\Rightarrow(2-a)^2+5^2=(10-a)^2+3^2\Rightarrow a=5.$$ (c) $$r^2=(2-5)^2+(3+2)^2=34\Rightarrow (x-5)^2+(y+2)^2=34.$$ (d) Solve $$y=4x-22$$ with circle: $$x=5\pm\sqrt2,\ y=-2\pm4\sqrt2;$$ so $$A\!\left(5+\sqrt2,\,-2+4\sqrt2\right),\ B\!\left(5-\sqrt2,\,-2-4\sqrt2\right).$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The points $$A(-1,9),~B(6,10),~C(7,3),~D(0,2)$$ lie on a circle. (a) Show $$ABCD$$ is a square. (b) Find its area. (c) Find the centre of the circle.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Show sides equal and perpendicular using vectors; centre is midpoint of diagonal.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: (a) $$\overrightarrow{AB}=(7,1),~\overrightarrow{BC}=(1,-7),$$ with $$|\overrightarrow{AB}|^2=|\overrightarrow{BC}|^2=50,$$ and $$\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=7(1)+1(-7)=0$$ ⇒ sides equal and perpendicular ⇒ square. (b) Area $$=\text{side}^2=50.$$ (c) Centre = midpoint of diagonal $$A,C$$: $$\Big(\frac{-1+7}{2},\frac{9+3}{2}\Big)=(3,6).$$ Radius $$r=\sqrt{50}/2=5.$$ Hence circle $$\boxed{(x-3)^2+(y-6)^2=25}. $$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The points $$D(-12,-3),~E(-10,b),~F(2,-5)$$ lie on a circle with $$\angle DEF=90^\circ$$ and $$b>0$$. (a) Find $$b$$. (b) Find the equation of the circle.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: For perpendicular lines: $$m_{DE}\cdot m_{EF}=-1$$; a right angle subtends a diameter ⇒ centre is midpoint of diameter $$DF$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: (a) $$m_{DE}=\frac{b+3}{2},~m_{EF}=\frac{-5-b}{12},~m_{DE}m_{EF}=-1\Rightarrow-\frac{(b+3)(b+5)}{24}=-1\Rightarrow b^2+8b-9=0.$$ So $$b=\frac{-8\pm\sqrt{100}}{2}=1,-9$$ and since $$b>0\Rightarrow\boxed{b=1}.$$ (b) Right angle at $$E$$ ⇒ diameter is $$DF$$. Centre $$O=\Big(\frac{-12+2}{2},\frac{-3+(-5)}{2}\Big)=(-5,-4).$$ Radius squared $$r^2=OD^2=(7)^2+(-1)^2=50.$$ Hence $$\boxed{(x+5)^2+(y+4)^2=50}.$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The circle has equation $$x^2+2x+y^2-24y-24=0.$$ (a) Find the centre and radius of the circle. (b) The points $$A(-13,17)$$ and $$B(11,7)$$ lie on the circumference. Show that $$AB$$ is a diameter. (c) The point $$C$$ lies on the negative x-axis and the angle $$ACB=90^\circ$$. Find the coordinates of $$C$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Complete the square to find the centre and radius; check that A,B satisfy the circle and midpoint equals centre. Use circle geometry (right angle in semicircle).
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: (a) Rewrite: $$(x^2+2x+1)+(y^2-24y+144)=24+1+144\Rightarrow(x+1)^2+(y-12)^2=169.$$ Hence centre $$(-1,12)$$ and radius $$13$$. (b) Midpoint of $$A,B$$ is $$\Big(\frac{-13+11}{2},\frac{17+7}{2}\Big)=(-1,12),$$ equal to centre ⇒ $$AB$$ is a diameter. (c) Right angle on semicircle ⇒ $$C$$ lies on circle and $$\angle ACB=90^\circ$$ ⇒ x-axis (y=0). Substitute $$y=0$$ in circle: $$(x+1)^2+(0-12)^2=169\Rightarrow x^2+2x+1+144=169\Rightarrow x^2+2x-24=0\Rightarrow(x+6)(x-4)=0,$$ so $$x=-6$$ or $$x=4$$. Negative x-axis ⇒ $$\boxed{C(-6,0)}.$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The circle $$C$$ has equation $$(x-3)^2+(y+3)^2=52.$$ The baselines $$l_1$$ and $$l_2$$ are tangents to the circle and have gradient $$\frac{4}{3}$$. (a) Find the points of intersection $$P,Q$$ of the tangents and the circle. (b) Find the equations of $$l_1$$ and $$l_2$$, giving your answers in the form $$ax+by+c=0.$$
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Use line form $$y=mx+c$$, substitute in circle, and use discriminant $$=0$$ to find possible $$c$$ values (tangent condition).

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The circle $$C$$ has equation $$x^2+6x+y^2-2y=7.$$ The lines $$l_1$$ and $$l_2$$ are tangents to the circle meeting at the point $$(10,6).$$ Find (a) the equations of $$l_1$$ and $$l_2$$, (b) the points of intersection $$P,Q$$ of the tangents with the circle, (c) the area of quadrilateral $$APRQ$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Find circle’s centre and radius by completing square, use tangent condition (discriminant = 0) to find slopes.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: (a) Complete the square: $$(x+3)^2+(y-1)^2=17,$$ centre $(-3,1)$, radius $\sqrt{17}$. Tangent form $y-6=m(x-10)$, substitute in circle, discriminant = 0: $$(x+3)^2+[m(x-10)+5]^2=17.$$ Expand and solve ⇒ quadratic in $x$: $$(1+m^2)x^2+2x[3+m(5-10m)] +[...] = 0.$$ Discriminant $=0$ ⇒ $$m^2+10m-3=0$$ ⇒ $$m_1=-5+2\sqrt{7},~m_2=-5-2\sqrt{7}.$$ (b) Substitute each $m$ into line equation to find $P,Q$. (c) Use coordinate geometry area formula for quadrilateral.

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The circle $$C$$ has centre $$(6,9)$$ and radius $$\sqrt{50}.$$ The line $$l$$ with equation $$x+y-21=0$$ intersects the circle at the points $$P,Q$$. (a) Find the coordinates of $$P$$ and $$Q$$. (b) Find equations of the tangents $$l_1$$ and $$l_2$$ at $$P,Q$$ respectively. (c) Find the equation of the line perpendicular bisector of chord $$PQ$$. (d) Show that the two tangents and the perpendicular bisector intersect at one point $$R$$, and find $$R$$. (e) Calculate the area of the kite $$APRQ$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Substitute $$y=21-x$$ into circle and solve; find tangent slopes from radii, then bisector and intersection.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: (a) Sub: $$(x-6)^2+(21-x-9)^2=50\Rightarrow(x-6)^2+(12-x)^2=50\Rightarrow2x^2-36x+180=50\Rightarrow2x^2-36x+130=0\Rightarrow x^2-18x+65=0.$$ Roots $$x=13,5$$ ⇒ $$P(13,8),~Q(5,16).$$ (b) Radii slopes: $$m_P=\frac{8-9}{13-6}=-\frac{1}{7}\Rightarrow m_{t1}=7,$$ $$m_Q=\frac{16-9}{5-6}=-7\Rightarrow m_{t2}=\frac{1}{7}.$$ Tangents: $$l_1: y-8=7(x-13)\Rightarrow7x-y-83=0,$$ $$l_2: y-16=\frac{1}{7}(x-5)\Rightarrow x-7y+107=0.$$ (c) Midpoint of $$PQ(9,12)$$, slope $$m_{PQ}=\frac{16-8}{5-13}=-1\Rightarrow m_\perp=1$$ ⇒ $$y-12=x-9\Rightarrow x-y+3=0.$$ (d) Solve $$7x-y-83=0,~x-y+3=0$$ ⇒ $$x=12.57,~y=15.57$$ ⇒ $$R(12.57,15.57).$$ All three intersect at $$R$$. (e) Use kite area formula with diagonals.

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The line $$y=-3x+12$$ meets the coordinate axes at $$A$$ and $$B$$. The line segment $$AB$$ is a diameter of a circle. Find the equation of the circle.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Find intercepts, midpoint, and radius from half the diagonal.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: Intercepts: at x-axis (y=0): $$x=4\Rightarrow A(4,0)$$; at y-axis (x=0): $$y=12\Rightarrow B(0,12).$$ Centre = midpoint $$O(2,6),$$ radius $$r^2=(4-2)^2+(0-6)^2=4+36=40.$$ Equation: $$\boxed{(x-2)^2+(y-6)^2=40.}$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The points $$A(-3,-2),~B(-6,0),~C(1,9)$$ lie on the circumference of a circle such that $$\angle ABC=90^\circ.$$ (a) Find the value of $$q$$. (b) Find the equation of the circle.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Use right-angle property ⇒ $$AC$$ is diameter, then midpoint gives centre and distance gives radius.

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The points $$R(-4,3),~S(7,4),~T(8,-7)$$ lie on the circumference of a circle. (a) Show that $$RT$$ is the diameter of the circle. (b) Find the equation of the circle.

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The points $$A(-4,0),~B(4,8),~C(6,0)$$ lie on the circumference of a circle. Find the equation of the circle.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Use perpendicular bisectors of two chords.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: Chord $$AB:~M_{AB}(0,4),~m_{AB}=\frac{8-0}{4-(-4)}=1\Rightarrow m_\perp=-1.$$ ⇒ $$y-4=-1(x-0)\Rightarrow x+y-4=0.$$ Chord $$BC:~M_{BC}(5,4),~m_{BC}=\frac{0-8}{6-4}=-4\Rightarrow m_\perp=\frac{1}{4}.$$ ⇒ $$y-4=\frac{1}{4}(x-5)\Rightarrow x-4y+11=0.$$ Solve: $$x+y-4=0,~x-4y+11=0\Rightarrow y=3,~x=1.$$ So centre $$(1,3).$$ Radius squared $$r^2=(1+4)^2+(3-0)^2=25+9=34.$$ Hence circle $$\boxed{(x-1)^2+(y-3)^2=34.}$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The points $$A(-7,7),\ B(1,9),\ C(3,1),\ D(-7,1)$$ lie on a circle. (a) Find the perpendicular bisector of (i) $$AB$$ (ii) $$CD$$. (b) Hence find the equation of the circle.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Use midpoint–slope for each chord: midpoint $$M=\big(\tfrac{x_1+x_2}{2},\tfrac{y_1+y_2}{2}\big)$$, slope $$m=\tfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$$, bisector slope $$m_\perp=-\tfrac1m$$ (vertical if segment is horizontal). Centre is intersection of the two bisectors; radius from any given point.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: (a)(i) $$M_{AB}=\Big(\tfrac{-7+1}{2},\tfrac{7+9}{2}\Big)=(-3,8),\ m_{AB}=\tfrac{9-7}{1-(-7)}=\tfrac14\Rightarrow m_\perp=-4.$$ Line through $$(-3,8):\ y-8=-4(x+3)\Rightarrow \boxed{\,4x+y+4=0\,}.$$ (ii) $$M_{CD}=\Big(\tfrac{3+(-7)}{2},\tfrac{1+1}{2}\Big)=(-2,1),\ m_{CD}=0$$ (horizontal) $$\Rightarrow$$ bisector is vertical: \boxed{$$x=-2$$}. (b) Centre $$O$$ at the intersection: from $$x=-2$$ in $$4x+y+4=0\Rightarrow y=4$$, so $$O(-2,4).$$ Radius squared from $$A$$: $$r^2=(\!-2+7)^2+(4-7)^2=5^2+(-3)^2=34.$$ Hence the circle is \boxed{$$(x+2)^2+(y-4)^2=34$$}.

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: Use $$\frac{A+B}{k}=\frac{A}{k}+\frac{B}{k}$$ term-by-term; or divide every term by the monomial/constant; collect like terms; allow negative exponents for leftover factors in the denominator.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: (a) Split and divide: $$\tfrac{4x^4}{x}=4x^3,\ \tfrac{5x^2}{x}=5x,\ \tfrac{-7x}{x}=-7\Rightarrow 4x^3+5x-7.$$ (b) First combine $$7x^5-5x^5=2x^5;$$ then divide by \(x\): $$\tfrac{2x^5}{x}=2x^4,\ \tfrac{9x^3}{x}=9x^2,\ \tfrac{x^2}{x}=x\Rightarrow 2x^4+9x^2+x.$$ (c) Divide by \(x^2\): $$\tfrac{-x^4}{x^2}=-x^2,\ \tfrac{4x^2}{x^2}=4,\ \tfrac{6}{x^2}=6x^{-2}\Rightarrow -x^2+4+6x^{-2}.$$ (d) Divide by \(x\): $$7x^4-x^2-\tfrac{4}{x}.$$ (e) Factor common \(2x\) in denominator and cancel per term: $$\tfrac{8x^4}{2x}=4x^3,\ \tfrac{-4x^3}{2x}=-2x^2,\ \tfrac{6x}{2x}=3\Rightarrow 4x^3-2x^2+3.$$ (f) Divide by \(3x\): $$\tfrac{9x^2}{3x}=3x,\ \tfrac{-12x^3}{3x}=-4x^2,\ \tfrac{-3x}{3x}=-1\Rightarrow -4x^2+3x-1.$$ (g) Order then split: $$\tfrac{-x^4}{5x}=-\tfrac15x^3,\ \tfrac{7x^3}{5x}=\tfrac75x^2,\ \tfrac{-2}{5x}=-\tfrac{2}{5x}\Rightarrow -\tfrac15x^3+\tfrac75x^2-\tfrac{2}{5x}.$$ (h) Divide by \(-2x\) carefully (signs!): $$\tfrac{-4x^2}{-2x}=2x,\ \tfrac{6x^4}{-2x}=-3x^3,\ \tfrac{-2x}{-2x}=1\Rightarrow -3x^3+2x+1.$$ (i) Divide by \(-2x\): $$\tfrac{-x^8}{-2x}=\tfrac12x^7,\ \tfrac{9x^4}{-2x}=-\tfrac92x^3,\ \tfrac{-4x^3}{-2x}=2x^2,\ \tfrac{6}{-2x}=-\tfrac3x\Rightarrow \tfrac12x^7-\tfrac92x^3+2x^2-\tfrac3x.$$ (j) Divide by \(-3x\): $$\tfrac{-9x^9}{-3x}=3x^8,\ \tfrac{-6x^6}{-3x}=2x^5,\ \tfrac{4x^4}{-3x}=-\tfrac43x^3,\ \tfrac{-2}{-3x}=\tfrac{2}{3x}\Rightarrow 3x^8+2x^5-\tfrac43x^3+\tfrac{2}{3x}.$$

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: It is claimed that the following inequality is true for all negative numbers $x$ and $y$: $x+y \ge \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$. A student's proof: $(x+y)^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}+2xy$, which is $\ge x^{2}+y^{2}$ since $2xy>0$ because $x$ and $y$ are both negative, so $xy$ is positive.(a)Explain the error made by the student.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: Check whether squaring preserves the direction of an inequality when the left side can be negative; also compare the signs of $x+y$ and $\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: $$\text{Error: For negative }x,y,\ \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}>0\text{ but }x+y<0,\ \text{so }x+y\ge\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}\text{ is already false. Squaring is only safe when both sides are nonnegative and the inequality actually holds. From }(x+y)^{2}\ge x^{2}+y^{2}\iff 2xy\ge0\text{ (true since }xy>0)\text{ one cannot conclude }x+y\ge\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}\text{ because }x+y<0\text{. The proof assumes a conclusion from a condition where squaring is invalid.}$$

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: (b) By use of a counter-example, verify that the inequality is not satisfied if both $x$ and $y$ are negative.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: Try a simple Pythagorean pair like $(-3,-4)$.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: $$\text{Take }x=-3,\ y=-4.\ \text{Then }x+y=-7\text{ and }\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}=\sqrt{9+16}=5.\ \text{Since }-7\not\ge5,\ \text{the claimed inequality fails when both are negative.}$$

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_title: Proving the inequality for positive values
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: (c) Prove that this inequality is true if $x$ and $y$ are both positive.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: Square both sides (now valid because both sides are nonnegative) and use $2xy>0$.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: $$\text{If }x,y>0,\ \text{then }(x+y)^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}+2xy>x^{2}+y^{2}.\ \text{Both sides are }\ge0,\ \text{so taking square roots gives }x+y>\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}.\ \text{Hence the inequality holds (with strict }>)\text{ for positive }x,y.$$

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: Given that $$-1$$ is a root of $$2x^{3}-5x^{2}-4x+3=0$$, find the two positive roots.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: Use the known root to factor out $$(x+1)$$ and then solve the remaining quadratic factor.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: Because $$-1$$ is a root, $$f(-1)=0$$ and $$(x+1)$$ is a factor of $$2x^{3}-5x^{2}-4x+3$$. Divide $$2x^{3}-5x^{2}-4x+3$$ by $$(x+1)$$: Step 1: $$\frac{2x^{3}}{x}=2x^{2}$$, so $$2x^{2}(x+1)=2x^{3}+2x^{2}$$ and subtract to get $$-7x^{2}-4x+3$$; Step 2: $$\frac{-7x^{2}}{x}=-7x$$, so $$-7x(x+1)=-7x^{2}-7x$$ and subtract to get $$3x+3$$; Step 3: $$\frac{3x}{x}=3$$, so $$3(x+1)=3x+3$$ and the remainder is $$0$$. Thus $$2x^{3}-5x^{2}-4x+3=(x+1)(2x^{2}-7x+3)$$. Solve $$2x^{2}-7x+3=0$$: discriminant $$\Delta=(-7)^{2}-4\cdot2\cdot3=49-24=25$$, so $$x=\dfrac{7\pm5}{4}=\dfrac{12}{4},\dfrac{2}{4}=3,\dfrac12$$. The two positive roots are $$x=3$$ and $$x=\dfrac12$$.

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: Prove that $$\dfrac{x-y}{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}}\equiv\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}$$ (for $$x\ge0,y\ge0,x\ne y$$).
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: Rationalise the denominator by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate $$\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}$$.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: Start with $$\dfrac{x-y}{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}}$$ and multiply by $$\dfrac{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}}$$: $$\dfrac{x-y}{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}}=\dfrac{(x-y)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})}{(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y})(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})}$$. The denominator simplifies using the difference of squares: $$(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y})(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})=x-y$$, so the fraction becomes $$\dfrac{(x-y)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})}{x-y}=\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}$$ (since $$x\ne y$$). Hence the identity holds.

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: Use completing the square to prove that $$n^{2}-8n+20$$ is positive for all values of $$n$$.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: Rewrite the quadratic as a perfect square plus a positive constant, and use that a square is always non-negative.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: Complete the square: $$n^{2}-8n+20=(n^{2}-8n+16)+4=(n-4)^{2}+4$$. For any real $$n$$, $$(n-4)^{2}\ge0$$, so $$(n-4)^{2}+4\ge4>0$$. Therefore $$n^{2}-8n+20$$ is positive for all values of $$n$$.

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: Prove that the quadrilateral $$A(1,1),\ B(3,2),\ C(4,0),\ D(2,-1)$$ is a square.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: Use the distance formula to show all four sides have equal length and show that adjacent sides are perpendicular (for example using dot products).
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: First find the side vectors: $$\overrightarrow{AB}=(3-1,2-1)=(2,1)$$, $$\overrightarrow{BC}=(4-3,0-2)=(1,-2)$$, $$\overrightarrow{CD}=(2-4,-1-0)=(-2,-1)$$, $$\overrightarrow{DA}=(1-2,1-(-1))=(-1,2)$$. Their squared lengths are $$|\overrightarrow{AB}|^{2}=2^{2}+1^{2}=5$$, $$|\overrightarrow{BC}|^{2}=1^{2}+(-2)^{2}=5$$, $$|\overrightarrow{CD}|^{2}=(-2)^{2}+(-1)^{2}=5$$, $$|\overrightarrow{DA}|^{2}=(-1)^{2}+2^{2}=5$$, so all sides are equal. Check perpendicularity: $$\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=2\cdot1+1\cdot(-2)=2-2=0$$, so angle at $$B$$ is a right angle. A quadrilateral with four equal sides and one right angle is a square, so $$ABCD$$ is a square.

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_title: Even sum of consecutive odd numbers
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: Prove that the sum of two consecutive positive odd numbers less than ten gives an even number.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: Represent two consecutive odd numbers in algebraic form and add them.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: Let the two consecutive positive odd numbers be $$2n+1$$ and $$2n+3$$, where $$n$$ is an integer and $$2n+3<10$$. Their sum is $$(2n+1)+(2n+3)=4n+4=4(n+1)$$, which is a multiple of $$4$$ and therefore even. Hence the sum of any two consecutive positive odd numbers (and in particular those less than ten) is an even number.

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: Prove that the statement “$$n^{2}-n+3$$ is a prime number for all values of $$n$$” is untrue.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: Find a specific integer value of $$n$$ for which $$n^{2}-n+3$$ is not prime.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: Take $$n=4$$. Then $$n^{2}-n+3=4^{2}-4+3=16-4+3=15$$. But $$15=3\times5$$ is not prime. So there exists at least one value of $$n$$ for which $$n^{2}-n+3$$ is not a prime number, and the statement “for all values of $$n$$” is therefore untrue.

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: Prove that $$(x-\frac{1}{x})(x^{\frac{4}{3}}+x^{-\frac{2}{3}})\equiv x^{\frac{1}{3}}\!\left(x^{2}-\frac{1}{x^{2}}\right).$$
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: Expand the left-hand side using distributive law and simplify using index laws $$x^{a}x^{b}=x^{a+b}$$.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: Start with $$(x-\frac{1}{x})(x^{\frac{4}{3}}+x^{-\frac{2}{3}})=x\cdot x^{\frac{4}{3}}+x\cdot x^{-\frac{2}{3}}-\frac{1}{x}\cdot x^{\frac{4}{3}}-\frac{1}{x}\cdot x^{-\frac{2}{3}}.$$ Using index laws, $$x\cdot x^{\frac{4}{3}}=x^{1+\frac{4}{3}}=x^{\frac{7}{3}},\quad x\cdot x^{-\frac{2}{3}}=x^{1-\frac{2}{3}}=x^{\frac{1}{3}},\quad \frac{1}{x}\cdot x^{\frac{4}{3}}=x^{\frac{4}{3}-1}=x^{\frac{1}{3}},\quad \frac{1}{x}\cdot x^{-\frac{2}{3}}=x^{-\frac{2}{3}-1}=x^{-\frac{5}{3}}.$$ Hence the expression becomes $$x^{\frac{7}{3}}+x^{\frac{1}{3}}-x^{\frac{1}{3}}-x^{-\frac{5}{3}}=x^{\frac{7}{3}}-x^{-\frac{5}{3}}$$. Factor out $$x^{\frac{1}{3}}$$: $$x^{\frac{7}{3}}-x^{-\frac{5}{3}}=x^{\frac{1}{3}}\!\left(x^{2}-\frac{1}{x^{2}}\right).$$ Thus $$(x-\frac{1}{x})(x^{\frac{4}{3}}+x^{-\frac{2}{3}})\equiv x^{\frac{1}{3}}\!\left(x^{2}-\frac{1}{x^{2}}\right).$$

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: Expand the right-hand side step by step and show that it simplifies to the left-hand side.

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: The equation $$x^{2}-kx+k=0$$, where $$k$$ is a positive constant, has two equal roots. Prove that $$k=4$$.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: For a quadratic $$ax^{2}+bx+c=0$$ to have equal roots, its discriminant $$b^{2}-4ac$$ must be zero.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: Here $$a=1$$, $$b=-k$$, $$c=k$$. Equal roots give $$b^{2}-4ac=0\Rightarrow(-k)^{2}-4\cdot1\cdot k=0\Rightarrow k^{2}-4k=0\Rightarrow k(k-4)=0$$. Since $$k$$ is positive, $$k\neq0$$, so $$k-4=0\Rightarrow k=4$$. Therefore the only positive value of $$k$$ for which the equation has equal roots is $$k=4$$.

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_title: Distance between opposite edges of a regular hexagon
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: Prove that the distance between opposite edges of a regular hexagon of side length $$\sqrt{3}$$ is a rational value.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: Use the fact that a regular hexagon can be divided into six equilateral triangles and relate the distance between opposite edges to the height of one such triangle.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: A regular hexagon of side length $$s$$ can be split into six equilateral triangles each of side $$s$$ with a common centre. The distance between opposite edges (the “flat-to-flat” distance) is twice the apothem (the perpendicular distance from the centre to a side). For an equilateral triangle of side $$s$$, the height (and so the apothem of the hexagon) is $$\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}s$$. Thus the distance between opposite edges is $$2\cdot\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}s=\sqrt{3}s$$. With $$s=\sqrt{3}$$, this distance is $$\sqrt{3}\cdot\sqrt{3}=3$$, which is a rational number. Hence the distance between opposite edges is rational.

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_title: Difference of squares of consecutive even numbers
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: Prove that the difference of the squares of two consecutive even numbers is always divisible by $$4$$.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: Represent consecutive even numbers as $$2n$$ and $$2n+2$$ and subtract their squares.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: Let the two consecutive even numbers be $$2n$$ and $$2n+2$$, where $$n$$ is an integer. Their squares are $$(2n)^{2}=4n^{2}$$ and $$(2n+2)^{2}=4n^{2}+8n+4.$$ The difference (larger minus smaller) is $$(2n+2)^{2}-(2n)^{2}=(4n^{2}+8n+4)-4n^{2}=8n+4=4(2n+1).$$ Since this is a multiple of $$4$$ for every integer $$n$$, the difference of the squares is always divisible by $$4$$.
